# Introduction

This vignette walks through the basic workflow of the ECLIPSE package.
Please refer to our 
[pre-print](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.02.18.706444v1)
for more details about this method.

## What is ECLIPSE? Why should I use it to analyze my scTCR-seq data?

Traditional analysis of single-cell TCR sequencing (scTCR-seq) data defines 
T cell clones based on the paired CDR3 sequences of the 
TCRα and TCRβ chains. However, as >50% of cells in some samples 
possess only 1 or >2 TCR chains, this approach is ill-suited to interpret the 
clonotypes of a substantial proportion of cells.

ECLIPSE builds on `r Biocpkg("VDJdive")` to address 
this limitation of standard scTCR-seq 
analysis. By analyzing chain pairings across a sample, it is able to resolve 
clonal ambiguity, allowing for the prediction of chains lost to dropout and the 
deciphering of true biological expression of extra TCR chains from technical 
artifacts. With less missing data and larger clone sizes, users are then able 
to make best use of their scTCR-seq data. The ECLIPSE workflow is also quite 
streamlined, typically utilizing just 2 core functions (`ECLIPSE` --> 
`tcrDoubletDetect`). After completing these two functions, users are ready
for convenient downstream analysis with the `r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")` 
package.


## What are the inputs to ECLIPSE? Is there any pre-processing required?

ECLIPSE has two main inputs. The first is all or filtered contig files that 
can be generated by running `cellranger vdj` or `cellranger multi` on 
scTCR-seq FASTQ files. The second is a Seurat object containing the cells in
the contig files. These are currently the only input types that 
ECLIPSE can directly utilize, however users who prefer scRNA-seq analysis 
packages other than Seurat can still use ECLIPSE by converting their object 
to a Seurat object. For example, a SingleCellExperiment object could be used. 
For more details on this conversion and an example, please see the 
supplemental information section.

## How is ECLIPSE different from other Bioconductor and non-Bioconductor scTCR-seq analysis packages?

ECLIPSE has similarities with other scTCR-seq analysis packages, but it also 
has many differences. Like many other packages, it defines individual TCR
chains by the CDR3 amino acid sequence and uses contig files from `cellranger`
for its input. However, in contrast to other packages, for cells that don't 
have a clear, unambiguous clonotype (i.e. 1 TCRα and 1 TCRβ), ECLIPSE 
examines chain pairings from other cells in the same sample to predict the 
most likely clonotype. Conventional packages (such as 
`r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")`) would instead filter the cell out,
leave the cell with missing chains, or only select the highest expressed chain
of each type. 

Another core distinction of ECLIPSE from other packages is it
is specifically designed to annotate clones with 3 TCR chains and discern true
biological expression of 3 TCR chains from sequencing artifacts such as 
doublets or TCR contamination. Standard packages either do not allow clones to 
have 3 TCR chains or do not distinguish true biological expression from 
sequencing artifacts.

ECLIPSE shares some features with another Bioconductor scTCR-seq analysis 
package, `r Biocpkg("VDJdive")`. `r Biocpkg("VDJdive")` implemented the EM 
algorithm to predict the clonotypes of cells with ambiguous clonotypes. ECLIPSE 
uses this implementation; however, there are some key differences 
between the packages. First, ECLIPSE utilizes custom contig filtering in 
order to preserve as many TCR chains as possible, while 
`r Biocpkg("VDJdive")` uses the filtered contigs from `cellranger`. ECLIPSE has
hard assignment of cells to clonotypes (i.e. each cell is assigned a single 
clonotype), whereas `r Biocpkg("VDJdive")` has soft assignment (i.e. 1 cell 
can be split into multiple different clonotypes). Lastly, ECLIPSE allows clones
to possess 2 or 3 TCR chains and integrates with `r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")` 
for downstream analysis and visualization, while `r Biocpkg("VDJdive")` permits
clones to have only 2 TCR chains and has its own visualization/analysis 
functionalities. Other differences exist, but these are the most important 
ones to understand.


# Installation and loading

We need to first load two packages to run the vignette:
```{r loadLibraries, results = "hide", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(tidyverse) # needed for data wrangling (or use base R instead)
library(scRepertoire) # needed for downstream analysis
```

Please use the following code to download `ECLIPSE` from Bioconductor and load it:
```{r githubInstall, eval = FALSE}
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("ECLIPSE")
```

```{r loadECLIPSE, eval = FALSE}
library(ECLIPSE)
```

Alternatively, use the following code to download the devel version of `ECLIPSE` from GitHub and load it:
```{r githubInstallDevel, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("eburns10/ECLIPSE")
```

```{r loadECLIPSEDevel}
library(ECLIPSE)
```

```{r loadKnitr, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
require(knitr)
```


# Test dataset
ECLIPSE includes a small test dataset of 1,000 cells from 2 patients (S3 and
S15) with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (derived from [Braun et al., 2021](
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccell.2021.02.013)). Each patient has two samples: 
one from tumor tissue and one from matched adjacent normal tissue. To load the
dataset in, we can use the following code:
```{r loadSeuratObject}
data("vignette_object", package = "ECLIPSE")
```


# Preparing inputs for `ECLIPSE`
2 main inputs are required for `ECLIPSE`: a Seurat object that contains 
scRNA-seq data and contig files from `cellranger vdj/multi` (preferably 
`all_contig_annotations.csv` files). 

## Contig files
The first input is contig files from `cellranger multi` or `cellranger vdj`, 
specifically `all_contig_annotations.csv` or `filtered_contig_annotations.csv`
files. **We strongly recommend using all_contig_annotations** files as the 
filtered contig files remove some biologically true contigs (ex.
TCRα chains that use the TRDV1 gene segment, [see here](
https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1286688)) as well as non-productive 
contigs. While these non-productive chains may not influence T cell antigen 
specificity, their presence in the contig files allows for enhanced fidelity  
of clonal tracking by `ECLIPSE`.

To feed the contig files into `ECLIPSE`, there are two options:

### Option 1: use folder paths
For this option, a vector of folder paths that contain contig files is needed. 
`ECLIPSE` will find the contig files within the folders you 
provide, however it requires that each folder only contains 1 set of contig
files (i.e. you cannot put the contig files from each sample into 1 folder).
In order to create a vector of folder paths, we can use the `list.dirs()`
function:

```{r getFolderPath}
# Finding where the vignette data for ECLIPSE is stored
vignette_dir <- system.file("extdata/vignette", package = "ECLIPSE")

# Generates the vector of folder paths and excludes the current directory
tcr_folder_paths <- list.dirs(path = vignette_dir, full.names = TRUE)[-1]
print(tcr_folder_paths)
```


### Option 2: use contig file paths
The second option also requires a vector of paths, but instead you specify
the full path to the contig file. This option would be better if you have many
contig files from different samples in one folder. 
To make the vector, here we can use `list.files()`:

```{r getFilePath}
# Generates the vector of file paths
contig_paths <- list.files(path = vignette_dir,
                           pattern = "all_contig", 
                           recursive = TRUE, 
                           full.names = TRUE)
contig_paths
```


## Seurat object meta.data
4 arguments of `ECLIPSE` must be provided column names from the Seurat 
meta.data: `original_barcode`, `batch`, `donor`, and `group`. We will create 
these columns now.

### Column to pass to `original_barcode`
This column must contain the original 10X barcode for each cell. Because many
scRNA-seq analysis pipelines add prefixes/suffixes to cell barcodes, this 
column is required so that the TCR contigs (which contain the original 10X
barcodes) can be matched to their respective cell in the Seurat object. 
Typically, barcodes will end with -1, but this may not always be true, such 
as if `cellranger aggr` was used. Always check your raw contig and counts 
files to be sure! 

For our dataset, the raw contig files have cell barcode suffixes of -1, so 
let's look at the barcodes in our Seurat object to see if they will match:
```{r checkBarcodes}
# Existing cell barcodes. They aren't the original!
head(rownames(vignette_object[[]]))
```

As you can see, they do not match. Let's change the suffixes to -1 and make a 
new column called `cell_barcode` that we can pass to the `original_barcode` 
argument of ECLIPSE:
```{r makeBarcodeColumn}
# Making a column with these barcodes where the suffix is -1
vignette_object$cell_barcode <- str_replace(rownames(vignette_object[[]]),
                                            pattern = "-.*$", 
                                            replacement = "-1")
head(vignette_object$cell_barcode) %>% as.vector()
```

### Column to pass to `batch`
This column tells `ECLIPSE` which contig file holds the TCR information for
each cell in the Seurat object. The position of the contig file in the vector
must be provided here (ex. 2, but not "2").
```{r checkContigPaths}
# Looking at the vector of file_paths
contig_paths
```

For example, `contig_paths[2]` holds a path for the TCR contigs for a cells
from the tumor of S15, so any cell from that sample must have 2 
(integer) but not "2" (character) in this new column. We can make this column, 
here called `index`, as such:
```{r makeBatchColumn}
# Since normal tissue from sample 15 is first (S15N), it is 1.
# Tumor tissue from 15 is next (S15T), so it is 2, etc...
vignette_object[[]] <- vignette_object[[]] %>% 
                           mutate(index = case_when(
                               Sample == "S15_N" ~ 1,
                               Sample == "S15_T" ~ 2,
                               Sample == "S3_N" ~ 3,
                               Sample == "S3_T" ~ 4))
    
# Checking the column
table(vignette_object$index)
```

### Column to pass to `donor`
Next, we need to tell `ECLIPSE` which donor (or mouse) each cell was from. As 
`ECLIPSE` calls clonotypes by utilizing chain pairing across a repertoire, the 
more cells that are available, the more accurate this prediction will be 
(regardless of time/condition/treatment). For this reason, a column is 
required to provide the donor/mouse. Even if we want to compare S3 tumor vs. 
normal and S15 tumor vs. normal downstream, here we must provide S3 and S15. 
Fortunately, this column is already created for us, and it should be already 
present in most real-world uses. Let's look at this column, called `donor`:
```{r checkDonorColumn}
# Show donor column
table(vignette_object$donor)
```

### Column to pass to `group`
Lastly, we need to tell `ECLIPSE` how we want the final clonal statistics 
(i.e. clone cell count, frequency, etc..) to be calculated after clones are 
called. For our example, either S15/S3 or S3T/S3N/S15T/S15N would be equally 
valid. If a clone is only 1 cell, then if we provide the donor, the 
frequency will be 1/500 vs. if we provide the sample, then it will be
1/250. **Please note that this column can and often will be the same as the **
**column passed to donor**. Let's choose by sample here, which again is 
already created for us through the column `Sample` (and typically will be 
created in most real cases):
```{r checkSampleColumn}
# Show Sample column
table(vignette_object$Sample)
```

# Running the `ECLIPSE` function

## Description of function
Now we are ready to run the `ECLIPSE` function to analyze our scTCR-seq data. 
Briefly, this function does the following:

1. Reading in contig data
2. Filtering contigs (i.e. must be in Seurat, high_confidence, not duplicated,
TCRα or TCRβ, have a valid CDR3, etc...)
3. Calling `findThreeChainClones` to find clones with biological expression of 
3 total TCR chains and modifying the contigs to address this
4. Utilizing the implementation of the EM algorithm in 
`r Biocpkg("VDJdive")`'s clonoStats() function. This function analyzes chain 
pairings across a sample to determine the probability of each potential chain 
pairing for cells possessing only 1 or >2 total TCR chains 
4. Determining the final clonotype (stored in a column called `CTaa`). If 
it is highly likely the cell is in 1 clone, then that clone is used. If no 
clonotype is predicted with high confidence, then clonal prediction is not 
performed, and the final clonotype is instead determined by 
`scRepertoire::combineTCR()` using parameters passed to `ECLIPSE` from the 
`combineTcrArgs` argument (see supplemental information section)
5. Formatting the object for downstream analysis with 
`r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")`

For a full list of columns added by ECLIPSE and their description, please 
refer to the supplemental information section.

## Running `ECLIPSE`
To run `ECLIPSE`, there are two options, depending on whether we generated a 
vector of folders containing contigs or contig file paths. If we want to use
a vector of folder paths, we can use the following code:
```{r runEclipseFolder}
# Option 1: Running with paths of folders containing contigs
object_after_ECLIPSE <- ECLIPSE(contig_type = "all",
                                contig_folder_paths = tcr_folder_paths,
                                seurat_object = vignette_object,
                                batch = "index",
                                donor = "donor",
                                group = "Sample",
                                original_barcode = "cell_barcode",
                                verbose = FALSE)
```

Note that we use the `contig_folder_paths` argument, omit the 
`contig_file_paths` argument, and `contig_type = "all"`. Together, this tells 
`ECLIPSE` to search for `all_contig_annotations.csv` files in the folders that 
we provide.

If we want to provide TCR contig file paths, we can use the 
`contig_file_paths` argument, omit the `contig_folder_paths` argument, and 
`contig_type = "manual"`:
```{r runEclipseFile, fig.alt = "Plot from ECLIPSE"}
# Option 2: Running with contig paths
object_after_ECLIPSE <- ECLIPSE(contig_type = "manual",
                                contig_file_paths = contig_paths,
                                seurat_object = vignette_object,
                                batch = "index",
                                donor = "donor",
                                group = "Sample",
                                original_barcode = "cell_barcode")
```

As seen above, by default (verbose = TRUE), `ECLIPSE` will print some key 
stats during filtering as well as a QC plot that shows how well clonal 
prediction went. For this experiment, most cells (shown in orange) received 
their final clonotype by prediction. Many of these cells also were fully 
assigned to one clone by the EM algorithm (i.e. y = 1), so overall the 
analysis went quite well. 

Let's take a look at the final clonotypes that `ECLIPSE` decided on, now 
stored in the `CTaa` column of the Seurat meta.data:
```{r checkClonotypes}
# Final ECLIPSE clonotype
head(object_after_ECLIPSE$CTaa) %>% as.vector()
```

We can also compare these final clonotypes to what traditional analysis 
would have determined, now stored in the `scR_CTaa` column: 
```{r checkTraditionalClonotypes}
# Clonotype from traditional analysis
head(object_after_ECLIPSE$scR_CTaa) %>% as.vector()
```

ECLIPSE also provides clone sizes and clonal proportions in the 
`clonalFrequency` and `clonalProportion columns,` respectively, with matched 
columns having a scR_prefix to show what would happen with traditional 
analysis. For a full list of columns added by `ECLIPSE`, please refer to the 
supplemental information section.

# Running `tcrDoubletDetect`
Now that the `ECLIPSE` function has been ran, we should now run the 2nd core 
ECLIPSE function, `tcrDoubletDetect`, to filter out cells with excessive TCR 
chains (these cells are likely a mix of doublets and cells with TCR 
contamination). Here we remove any cells with >2 TCRα chains, >2 
TCRβ chains, or >4 total (α + β) chains:
```{r runDoubletDetect, fig.alt = "Plots from tcrDoubletDetect"}
object_after_ECLIPSE <- tcrDoubletDetect(object_after_ECLIPSE,
                                         singleChainLimit = 2,
                                         totalChainLimit = 4)
```
This function by default also prints plots that may be useful in setting
additional filtering thresholds. Here we can see that cells with 4 total TCR 
chains have much higher RNA counts, so we may want to remove these cells or 
any cells with ~ >7k nCount_RNA as they may be enriched for doublets. 

# Downstream analysis with `r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")`
At this point we're ready for downstream analysis. ECLIPSE generates Seurat
objects formatted for use with the popular `r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")` 
package, so functions introduced in that package typically can be used here 
as well. One key thing to note is that since `ECLIPSE` predicts clones based 
on CDR3 amino acid sequences, we must always use the argument 
`cloneCall = "aa"` in scRepertoire functions. 

Shown below are a couple potential types of downstream analysis made possible
with `r Biocpkg("scRepertoire")`. For example, we can look at clonal sharing 
across samples:
```{r runCompareClonotypes, fig.alt = "Plot showing clone sharing"}
clonalCompare(object_after_ECLIPSE,
              top.clones = 10,
              graph = "alluvial",
              cloneCall = "aa",
              group.by = "Sample") +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

```

We can also visualize which samples have a larger fraction of expanded 
clonotypes:
```{r runClonalHomeostasis, fig.alt = "Plot showing clone sizes"}
clonalHomeostasis(object_after_ECLIPSE,
                  cloneCall = "aa",
                  group.by = "Sample")
```

Or we can look at repertoire diversity across samples:
```{r runClonalDiversity, fig.alt = "Plot showing TCR diversity"}
clonalDiversity(object_after_ECLIPSE,
                metric = "shannon",
                cloneCall = "aa",
                group.by = "Sample")
```

# Conclusions
We hope this vignette is a helpful introduction to using ECLIPSE. If you have 
any questions, please email ethan.burns [@] yale.edu or use our issues 
[page](https://github.com/eburns10/ECLIPSE/issues). For more details about 
our method, please refer to our 
[pre-print](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.02.18.706444v1).


# Supplemental information

## Using ECLIPSE with single-cell objects other than Seurat
ECLIPSE can only operate with Seurat objects; however, you can still use 
ECLIPSE even if you prefer not to do most of your analysis with Seurat. To do 
so, you can use the following steps: 

1. Convert your object to a `Seurat` object
2. Run `ECLIPSE` on your `Seurat` object
3. Convert the `Seurat` object back to the type you started with, or 
alternatively extract the columns you would like from the `Seurat` meta.data 
and add them to your original object

Here we will show how this looks using Bioconductor's preferred format, 
the `SingleCellExperiment` object.

First, we load our required packages:
```{r, loadScePackage, results = "hide", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(Seurat)
```

```{r makeSCE, echo = FALSE, results = "hide", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
### Make a SingleCellExperiment object that mirrors our vignette object
sce_obj <- as.SingleCellExperiment(vignette_object)
```

### Step 1: Convert object to Seurat object
We can use the `as.Seurat` function here. The argument `data = NULL` is needed 
since our `SingleCellExperiment` object doesn't have a logcounts assay, 
but this may not always be the case.
```{r, convertToSeurat}
new_seurat <- as.Seurat(sce_obj, data = NULL)
```

### Step 2: Run `ECLIPSE`
This is identical to the standard approach.
```{r, runECLIPSE}
# 1: Get contig folder paths
vignette_dir <- system.file("extdata/vignette", package = "ECLIPSE")
tcr_folder_paths <- list.dirs(path = vignette_dir, full.names = TRUE)[-1]

#2: Make a column that has the original cell barcodes
new_seurat$cell_barcode <- str_replace(rownames(new_seurat[[]]),
                                       pattern = "-.*$", 
                                       replacement = "-1")

#3: Make a column to pass to batch
new_seurat[[]] <- new_seurat[[]] %>% 
    mutate(index = case_when(
        Sample == "S15_N" ~ 1,
        Sample == "S15_T" ~ 2,
        Sample == "S3_N" ~ 3,
        Sample == "S3_T" ~ 4))

#4: Make a column to pass to donor (already done for us here)
table(new_seurat$donor)

#5: Make a column to pass to sample (already done for us here)
table(new_seurat$Sample)

#6: Run ECLIPSE
new_seurat_with_tcr <- ECLIPSE(contig_type = "all",
                               contig_folder_paths = tcr_folder_paths,
                               seurat_object = new_seurat,
                               batch = "index",
                               donor = "donor",
                               group = "Sample",
                               original_barcode = "cell_barcode",
                              verbose = FALSE)
```

### Step 3: Convert back to old format or extract columns of interest and merge
The easiest way to return back to the original object is by simply converting 
the Seurat object back to the starting object type. For example:
```{r, returnToSceObject}
sce_obj_with_tcr <- as.SingleCellExperiment(new_seurat_with_tcr)

### Check original column names in SingleCellExperiment objects
colnames(sce_obj@colData)

### Check new column names in SingleCellExperiment object
colnames(sce_obj_with_tcr@colData)
```
As you can see, our starting object now has TCR information and all
metadata columns that are added by `ECLIPSE`.

It is possible that this approach may lead to the loss of some information 
other than cell metadata due to the conversion functions not being able to 
transfer all elements of the objects between types. To prevent this, you can 
also manually extract the `Seurat` meta.data columns of interest before  
analyzing them separately or joining them back to the original object. This 
preserves the original object and only adds the metadata columns that are 
desired. For example:
```{r, returnToSceObject2}
### Extract meta.data
tcr_meta <- new_seurat_with_tcr[[]] %>%
    select(Cell_barcode,
        highConfChains,
        scR_CTaa,
        CTaa,
        clonalProportion,
        clonalFrequency,
        cloneSize,
        cloneCallSource)

### Join with original meta.data
new_meta <- as.data.frame(colData(sce_obj)) %>%
    left_join(tcr_meta, by = "Cell_barcode") %>%
    column_to_rownames("Cell_barcode")

### Add joined meta.data to original object
colData(sce_obj) <- S4Vectors::DataFrame(new_meta)

### Check to confirm TCR data is now present
colnames(sce_obj@colData)
```


## Helper function: `findThreeChainClones`
While not discussed above, ECLIPSE contains a third function that may
may be of use. This function was designed to help the `ECLIPSE` function
find clones with biological expression of 3 TCR chains, but can be also
used to see which clones were called with 3 TCR chains and how that occurred.
To see these clones we can use the code below. First, we generate QC filtered
contigs using the `returnFilteredContigs` argument of `ECLIPSE`:
```{r makeContigs}
postqc_contigs <- ECLIPSE(contig_type = "all",
                          contig_folder_paths = tcr_folder_paths,
                          seurat_object = vignette_object,
                          batch = "index",
                          donor = "donor",
                          group = "Sample",
                          original_barcode = "cell_barcode",
                          verbose = FALSE,
                          returnFilteredContigs = TRUE)
```

Next, we filter on a sample we are interested in, and pass the contigs onto
`findThreeChainClones` using ` mode = "show"` and `chain = "a"`
to show clones with 2 TCRα chains:
```{r runFindThreeChainClones}
s15_contigs <- postqc_contigs %>% filter(donor == "S15")

three_chain_clones <- findThreeChainClones(s15_contigs,
                                           chain = "a",
                                           mode = "show",
                                           printStats = TRUE)
```

This provides a list containing:

1. A table of all clones with 2 TCRα chains after filtering
```{r getOutput1}
three_chain_clones[[1]]
```

2. Pre-filtering table that shows how some of these clones were called
```{r getOutput2}
three_chain_clones[[2]]
```




## `ECLIPSE` additional arguments

```{r makeArgsTable, echo = FALSE}
args <- c("`verbose`",
            "`returnFilteredContigs`",
            "`allowDoubleChains`",
            "`combineTcrArgs`",
            "`detailedEclipseStats`",
            "`format`")

descriptions <- c(
    paste(
        "By default `TRUE`. Prints stats such as QC filtering efficacy,",
        "how many clones were called with 3 chains, and final percentages",
        "of cells with a TCR called"
    ),
    paste(
        "By default `FALSE`. `TRUE` would return the contigs after",
        "QC filtering"
    ),
    paste(
        "By default `\"both\"`, whereby clones can have 2 TCRα or",
        "TCRβ chains. If `\"alpha\"` or `\"beta\"` is provided, only",
        "clones with 2 of that type will be permitted. If `\"neither\"` is", 
        "provided, then only clones with 2 chains will be called"
    ),
    paste(
        "A list that determines how `scRepertoire::combineTCR()` is called.",
        "As `ECLIPSE` runs `combineTCR/combineExpression` to allow users to",
        "combine the predicted `ECLIPSE` clonotype with a",
        "traditionally-defined clonotype, this tells which arguments",
        "`combineTCR` should be run with. Specifically, it tells the 4",
        "arguments 1) `removeNA`, 2) `removeMulti`, 3) `filterMulti`, and 4)", 
        "`filterNonproductive` in that order. If `ECLIPSE` cannot call a",
        "clonotype with high accuracy, the clonal annotation from this will",
        "be used as the final clonotype. By default, this is",
        "`list(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)`, which calls `combineTCR` with its",
        "default arguments (i.e. no non-productive contigs are retained but",
        "clones with 1 TCR chain or >2 are allowed)"
    ),
    paste(
        "By default `FALSE`. This adds information about the EM algorithm",
        "assignment to the Seurat object (i.e. what proportion of the cell",
        "was assigned to the clone listed, etc...)"
    ),
    paste(
        "By default `\"Blank\"`. This tells how missing data is stored in", 
        "contig files. Typically this is `\"\"` so `\"Blank\"` should be",
        "specified, however older versions of Cell Ranger use `\"None\"`",
        "instead. If this is the case, please provide `\"None\"` here"
    )
)

argsTable <- data.frame("Argument" = args,
                        "Description" = descriptions)
kable(argsTable, caption = "Additional arguments for the ECLIPSE function")
```


## Seurat object columns description

```{r makeColsTable, echo = FALSE}
cols <- c("`highConfChains`",
            paste("`scR_CTgene`, `scR_CTnt`, `scR_CTaa`, `scR_CTstrict`,",
                "`scR_conalProportion`, `scR_clonalFrequency`,",
                "`scR_cloneSize`"),
            "`cloneCallSource`",
            "`CTaa`, `clonalProportion`, `clonalFrequency`, `cloneSize`",
            "`cell_unconventional_subset`, `clone_unconventional_subset`",
           "`EM_max_prop`, `EM_2ndmax_prop`, `EM_max_2ndmax_ratio`")

descriptions <- c(
    paste("all TCR chains that were sequenced in the cell and passed QC",
        "filtering by `ECLIPSE`. Helpful to compare to final clone (`CTaa`)",
        "used for analysis"),
    paste("columns added by `scRepertoire::combineExpression`, see",
        BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scRepertoire"),
        "documentation for details. These",
        "provide information about the cell if it was called with",
        BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scRepertoire"),
        "and can be useful in comparing to the final clone",
        "(`CTaa`) used for analysis. Please note the \"scR_\" prefix is added",
        "so ECLIPSE can add other columns with the same name that can",
        "interact with scRepertoire"),
    paste("whether the final clonotype list (in `CTaa`) is from",
        "the prediction of ",
        BiocStyle::Biocpkg("VDJdive"),
        "or from traditional analysis from",
        BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scRepertoire")),
    paste("columns in the style of what would be added by",
        "`scRepertoire:::combineExpression`. However, `CTaa` here stores",
        "the final clonotype of the cell as predicted by `ECLIPSE`"),
    paste("`cell_unconventional_subset` tells if the chains detected suggest",
        "the cell is a iNKT or MAIT cell. `clone_unconventional_subset` gives",
        "similar information, but uses the final clonotype of the cell",
        "instead of what chains were detected in that particular cell (and",
        "therefore will capture more cells as being a iNKT or MAIT cell). For",
        "both of these columns, `ECLIPSE` searches for 3 subsets: 1) iNKT",
        "cells (must have TRAV10 + TRAJ18 + TRBV25-1), 2) conventional MAIT",
        "cells (must have TRAV1-2 + TRAJ33), and 3) unconventional MAIT cells",
        "(must have TRAV1-2 + TRAJ12 or TRAV1-2 + TRAJ20. Please note that",
        "these are for human samples only, murine T cells use different gene",
        "segments that are not searched for by `ECLIPSE`"),
    paste("the proportion of the cell assigned by the EM algorithm to the",
          "most and 2nd most likely clone. The ratio of these two proportions",
          "(biggest/2nd biggest) is also provided. These columns are only",
          "included if `detailedEclipseStats == TRUE`")
)

colsTable <- data.frame("Column" = cols,
                        "Description" = descriptions)

kable(colsTable, caption = "Columns made by the ECLIPSE function")
```
